newsitem.title: KENYA: Sugar for Rwanda, Burundi diverted to Kenya market.
newsitem.headline: Sugar for Rwanda, Burundi diverted to Kenya market.

text.p: Kenya's sugar supply is being swelled illegally as shipments meant for neighbouring countries are diverted into Kenyan retail shops, officials said.
Ports officials said on Wednesday hundreds of thousands of tonnes meant for Rwanda, Rwandan refugee camps in eastern Zaire and for Burundi were finding their way into the Kenyan market.
Kenya Ports Authority data show imports of 105,270 tonnes in the January-September period, compared with total imports in 1995 of 227,974 tonnes and 147,000 in 1994.
The planning ministry says imports have been much higher.
The authority gave the import figures on Wednesday after the Kenya Revenue Authority (KRA) launched a crackdown on tax evaders and corrupt traders diverting sugar meant to be in transit.
On Tuesday, Agriculture Minister Simeon Nyachae said corruption and poor policing was helping illegal imports into Kenya, avoiding taxes imposed to protect domestic producers.
Nyachae said, "Sugar meant to be on transit is getting into the market. The problem is these people have the right papers, we cannot do a thing."
On Monday, KRA officials seized more than 25,000 tonnes of sugar at a warehouse in Mombasa and sought verification that it was in transit for neighbouring countries.
Last week, KRA officers impounded 7,400 tonnes of sugar they said was also meant to be on transit.
They said they were monitoring sugar movement at the port because of rising incidents of transit sugar being diverted to domestic use.

On Tuesday, a ship was offloading 20,000 tonnes of sugar but no one would say whether it was for the Kenyan market or for onward shipment to Rwanda or to be held in warehouses pending the lifting of regional sanctions on Burundi.
In the last month, some 60,000 tonnes of sugar have been offloaded at Mombasa specifically for the Kenyan market.
An official at the Mumias Sugar Company, Kenya's chief miller, said they were unable to sell 20,000 tonnes of sugar imported in June because the domestic market was flooded.
The Kenya Sugar Authority has put production at 384,171 tonnes in 1995, from 303,292 tonnes in 1994, and sees a jump to 420,000 in 1996.
The Sugar Authority says domestic demand has risen steadily to 560,000 tonnes this year, from 348,678 in 1984.

Francis Chahonyo, chief executive at the sugar authority, last week wrote to the ports authority demanding details of all sugar imports so that the authority could track down importers who evaded taxes.

Ports documents showed imports from Brazil, Thailand, Romania, India, Britain, Belgium and Paraguay. Thailand was the main source, at 39,849 tonnes so far this year. Brazil's contribution was down to 9,012 tonnes from a total of 101,236 last year.
Kenya levies value added tax on sugar imports at six percent, a sugar development levy of 20 percent, a 25 percent ad valorem tax and a variable dumping duty of $105.83 per tonne of imported sugar.
